headline: AWS Blocks simplifies building AI chatbots with RAG pipelines
summary: New AWS Blocks framework treats infrastructure, backend, and frontend code as views of the same application, streamlining AI development.
details: Building AI applications that answer questions using private data, known as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), typically requires integrating multiple AWS services like S3, document extraction tools, vector storage, and Bedrock. This complex setup presents challenges in development, deployment, and local testing.

AWS Blocks aims to simplify this by unifying infrastructure, backend APIs, and frontend code within a single project. Instead of separate repositories for CDK projects, Lambda functions, and SDKs, AWS Blocks encourages a vertical slice approach where each feature is built cohesively.

The framework introduces an 'Infrastructure from Code' (IFC) paradigm, inverting the traditional 'Infrastructure as Code' (IaC) model. With IFC, application code defines the necessary infrastructure, rather than the other way around. This means a single building block contains everything needed for all environments.

A key feature is that imports behave differently based on the environment, eliminating the need for explicit conditional logic within the application code. This dynamic resolution simplifies local development and ensures consistency across different deployment stages.

The KnowledgeBase component in AWS Blocks not only provisions AWS resources but also exposes a runtime API directly callable from the application. This integrated approach removes the manual effort of creating Lambda functions, API Gateway routes, and frontend SDKs, streamlining the entire process.

headline_marked: [[Bananas sprout]] in UK gardens after 15 years due to warmer climate
headline: Bananas sprout in UK gardens after 15 years due to warmer climate
summary: Warmer summers and milder winters are enabling heat-loving plants like bananas to flourish in the UK, while traditional crops decline.
details: Tropical plant enthusiasts in Rayleigh, Essex, were astonished to see fruit finally grow on their 200 banana plants after 15 years, a feat previously rare in the UK.

The Royal Horticultural Society notes that heat-loving plants such as olives, figs, and apricots are excelling, while traditional British crops like gooseberries and rhubarb are declining in some areas.
Chief horticulturist Guy Barter stated that bananas never used to flower 20 years ago, but warmer climates are now making it possible for them to fruit.
While the Musa Basjoo banana is known for surviving UK winters, its flowers often need protection from frost. The Stavs have built walls around their plants to trap heat and create a microclimate.
Despite not wrapping their nearly 10ft tall plants in recent winters, the heatwave this year led to fruiting. Banana plants also propagate easily, producing more plants over time.
Similar reports have emerged from Suffolk, where a banana plant produced fruit for the first time after years of being grown for its aesthetic appeal.
Botanist James Wong explained that hotter UK temperatures make growing bananas 'very easy,' as they are fast-growing with sufficient heat and can tolerate ample watering and fertilization.
Wong advised that in colder or exposed areas, wrapping the stems can create an insulating layer to protect against frost damage.
While growing bananas in the UK is not entirely new for plant enthusiasts, it is becoming more accessible to the average person due to changing climate conditions.
